## Practical Notes on the Demos

Beyond the compute ceiling above, three things actually bite:

- **`peft` and `trl` break across versions.** Pin them in the handout and rerun the notebook the week before class; this is the single most common way a lab fails in the room.
- **The first weight download often takes longer than the inference**, so the notebook has to be warmed up before class. Nothing here needs a large dataset — a few hundred examples is enough for every lab.
- **The failure demos are the most memorable part of the course**, and three of them are worth the preparation time above all others: a reward with a deliberate hole in it, which the model finds within a few dozen RL steps (W9); a hidden hint in the prompt that changes the answer while the chain of thought never mentions it (W10); and an agent broken by indirect prompt injection (W13). Each is about thirty lines of code, and each settles an argument that would otherwise take ten papers.

## Four Things This Course Admits It Does Not Know

These gaps are load-bearing rather than embarrassing — each is a project topic, and saying so is the honest graduate-level position.

- **W2** — there is no verifiable published work on Traditional Chinese token efficiency. The fertility comparison has to be demonstrated live.
- **W12** — chunking and query rewriting have no citable representative papers; both are engineering folklore more than literature, so the course substitutes an ablation lab. RAG evaluation has fragmented, and nothing has become the accepted successor to RAGAS.
- **W13** — no textbook (JM3 ch 12 is unwritten), and no canonical design paper for the Model Context Protocol; its academic literature is almost entirely about security.
- **W14** — item response theory for benchmarks is still scattered; the text-side benchmarks for Taiwanese Hokkien and Hakka are effectively absent; and model welfare has no citable academic literature.
